intro: What a large language model actually is, why it sometimes makes things up, and what "thinking" means.

1.summary: Tokens, training vs inference, hallucination and knowledge cutoffs.

lesson.title: Autocomplete, but enormous
lesson.body:
A **large language model (LLM)** is a program trained on a huge amount of text to do one thing: predict the next **token** (a chunk of text, about ¾ of a word). Do that over and over and you get paragraphs, code and answers.

There are two very different phases:

- **Training**: months of expensive computing where the model learns patterns from text. Done once per model version by the lab (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google...).
- **Inference**: *using* the trained model, which is every time you send a message. You pay per token for this.

The model doesn't learn from your chats as you go. Each version is frozen after training.
lesson.pm: Almost all AI product costs you control are inference costs, and they scale with tokens. Long prompts and long outputs cost more on every single request.

lesson.title: Why it makes things up
lesson.body:
A **hallucination** is when a model states something false with total confidence. It happens because the model generates *plausible* text. It isn't looking facts up in a database.

Models also have a **knowledge cutoff**: they know nothing after their training data ends, unless you give it to them.

Ways to reduce hallucination:

- Put the real facts in the prompt (give it the doc, the data, the code)
- Let it use tools, like search or reading files
- Ask it to cite where each claim came from
- Verify anything important
lesson.pm: "How do we ground it?" (meaning: give it real sources) should be one of the first questions in any AI feature review.

cards.back: Large language model: an AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it write, answer and code.
A chunk of text (about ¾ of a word). Models read and write in tokens, and you pay per token.
The expensive, one-time process where a lab teaches a model from huge amounts of data.
Using a trained model, i.e. every request you send. Billed per token.
When a model confidently states something false, because it generates plausible text rather than looking up facts.
The date a model's training data ends. It doesn't know later events unless you tell it.

quiz.q: At its core, what is an LLM trained to do?
options: Predict the next token of text
Copy answers from the internet in real time
quiz.why: Everything an LLM does comes from repeatedly predicting the next token.

quiz.q: Your team's AI feature costs rise every time users send longer messages. That's because you pay for…
quiz.why: Every request is inference, and it's priced by input and output tokens.

quiz.q: A model confidently cites a research paper that doesn't exist. What's that called?
quiz.why: Confident but false output is a hallucination.

quiz.q: Best way to get accurate answers about your company's refund policy?
options: Put the actual policy text in the prompt (or let it retrieve it)
quiz.why: Grounding the model in real source material is the most reliable fix for hallucination.

quiz.q: Do models learn from your conversations as you chat?
options: No. A model version is frozen after training; within a chat it only uses the context you give it
quiz.why: The model's knowledge is fixed at training time. Apps can *remember* things by re-sending them as context, but the model itself doesn't change.

2.summary: System prompts, post-training, fine-tuning, reasoning and statelessness.

lesson.title: How models get their personality
lesson.body:
**Pre-training** gives a model raw knowledge from huge amounts of text. On its own that makes a clever autocomplete, not a helpful assistant.

**Post-training** turns it into an assistant. One well-known method is **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback): people, or other AIs, rate answers, and the model learns to give the better kind.

Then, as a builder, you shape it further:

- **System prompt**: standing instructions from the app builder that the end user usually doesn't see ("You are a friendly support agent for Acme…").
- **Fine-tuning**: extra training on your own examples. It's powerful but slower and costlier, and usually *not* the first thing to try. Better prompts and better context solve most problems.
lesson.pm: If someone proposes fine-tuning first, ask: "Have we exhausted prompting and giving it better context?" That's usually cheaper, faster and easier to change.

lesson.title: Thinking, statelessness and multimodal
lesson.body:
**Reasoning** (or **thinking**) models write out hidden scratch-work tokens before answering. That makes them better at hard, multi-step problems, but slower and more expensive. Many apps let you set an **effort** level.

Models are **stateless**: each request starts from zero. A chat "remembers" because the app re-sends the whole conversation every time. That's why long chats get slower and cost more.

**Multimodal** models take more than text: images, PDFs, screenshots, sometimes audio.
lesson.pm: Statelessness explains a lot of AI product behavior: why memory features exist, why long conversations get expensive, and why context management is a real engineering problem.

cards.back: Standing instructions from the app builder that shape the model's behavior, usually hidden from end users.
Training after pre-training that makes a model a helpful assistant, e.g. by learning from ratings of its answers.
Extra training on your own examples to specialize a model. Try prompting and better context first.
The model generating hidden scratch work before answering: better on hard problems, slower and pricier.
The model remembers nothing between requests. Apps re-send the conversation each time.
Able to take in more than text, like images, PDFs or audio.

quiz.q: Your support bot keeps being too formal. What should you try first?
options: Train a new model from scratch
quiz.why: Tone and behavior are usually quick system prompt changes. Fine-tuning is heavier and rarely the first move.

quiz.q: Why do long chat conversations get slower and more expensive?
options: The app re-sends the whole conversation on each turn because models are stateless
Longer chats use a bigger model
quiz.why: Every turn includes all previous turns as input tokens.

quiz.q: When is turning up reasoning/thinking effort worth the cost?
options: For hard, multi-step problems like tricky debugging or planning
quiz.why: Extra thinking pays off on hard tasks. On simple ones it mostly adds cost and delay.

options: Teaches a pre-trained model to give the kinds of answers people rate as helpful
quiz.why: Reinforcement learning from human feedback shapes behavior using ratings of answers.

quiz.q: You paste a screenshot of an error into Claude and it reads it. That's because the model is…
quiz.why: Multimodal models accept images and other inputs, not just text.
